cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK I
Athena comes to Ithaca;\nTelemachus resolves to seek his father.
Tell me the man, Muse — the man\nof many turnings, who was driven
wandering far, once he had sacked Troy's holy citadel:
many were the cities of men he saw,\nand he learned their minds,
many the griefs he suffered at heart on the open sea,
striving to win his own life\nand his companions' homecoming.
Even so he could not save them, hard though he strove:
they perished by their own recklessness,\nfools, who ate the cattle of Helios Hyperion,
and the god took from them their day of homecoming.
Begin where you will, goddess,\ndaughter of Zeus — tell us, too, the tale.
By then all the others, all who had escaped sheer ruin,\nwere home, safely past the war and past the sea.
Him alone — aching for homecoming and his wife —
the queenly nymph Calypso,\nshining among goddesses, held back
in her hollow caves, hungry to make him her husband.
But when the year came, in the wheeling round of seasons,
in which the gods had spun the thread of his return\nhome to Ithaca — not even there was he free of trials,
even among his own. And the gods pitied him,\nall but Poseidon: he raged without rest
against godlike Odysseus,\nuntil the day he reached his own land.
But now Poseidon was gone among the far-off Ethiopians —
the Ethiopians, sundered in two, remotest of mankind,\nhalf where Hyperion sets and half where he rises —
to receive a hecatomb of bulls and rams, and there\nhe sat at the feast, delighting. But the other gods
were gathered together in the halls of Olympian Zeus,
and among them the father of men and gods began to speak,\nfor his heart was remembering blameless Aegisthus,
whom Agamemnon's son, far-famed Orestes, killed.
Remembering him, he spoke among the immortals:
"Shameful! — how mortals lay their blame upon the gods.
From us, they say, all evils come — while they themselves,
by their own recklessness,\nearn griefs beyond their portion:
as Aegisthus now, beyond his portion, took to wife
the wedded bride of Atreus' son,\nand killed the man at his homecoming,
knowing it meant sheer ruin — for we told him beforehand,
sending Hermes down, the sharp-eyed slayer of Argus,\nnot to kill the man and not to court his wife:
for vengeance for the son of\nAtreus would come from Orestes
the day he came of age and longed for his own land.
So Hermes spoke, meaning him well —\nbut the mind of Aegisthus
he could not turn. Now he has\npaid for everything at once."
Then the goddess answered him, gray-eyed Athena:
"Father of us all, son of Cronos, highest of the mighty,\nthat man, yes, lies in a ruin he richly earned —
so may any other perish who does such things.
But my heart is on fire for battle-wise Odysseus,\nill-starred man, who far from his own people suffers long
on a sea-ringed island, at the navel of the sea.
A wooded island; a goddess has her dwelling there,\nthe daughter of Atlas the deadly-minded, he who knows
the depths of every sea, and himself grips the pillars,\nthe tall ones, that hold earth and heaven apart.
It is his daughter who keeps that broken, grieving man,
and always with soft words, with winding, coaxing words,\nshe charms him to forget Ithaca. But Odysseus,
who would be glad to see even the smoke go leaping\nup from his own country, aches to die. And your heart
does not turn for it, Olympian. Did Odysseus never\nplease you, offering sacrifice beside the Argive ships
in wide Troy? Why so at odds with Odysseus, Zeus?"
Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered her:
"My child, what a word has\nslipped the fence of your teeth!
How could I ever forget godlike Odysseus,\nwho is beyond all mortals in mind, and beyond all others gave
offerings to the deathless gods who hold wide heaven?
No: it is Poseidon who holds the earth, in anger
unbending, always, for the Cyclops,\nwhose one eye Odysseus blinded —
godlike Polyphemus, whose power is greatest among\nall the Cyclopes. The nymph Thoösa bore him,
daughter of Phorcys, a lord of the barren salt sea,\nwhen in her hollow caves she lay with Poseidon.
Ever since, Poseidon the shaker of earth does not kill
Odysseus, but drives him wandering from his father's land.
But come, let all of us here take careful thought together
for his homecoming — how he shall come. Poseidon\nwill let go his anger. He cannot, against us all,
wrangle alone in the teeth of the deathless gods."
Then the goddess answered him, gray-eyed Athena:
"Father of us all, son of Cronos, highest of the mighty,\nif this now truly pleases the blessed gods,
that Odysseus of the many designs\ncome home to his own house,
then let us dispatch Hermes, the guide, the slayer of\nArgus, to the island Ogygia, so that with all speed
he may tell the nymph of the\nlovely braids our fixed decree:
the homecoming of enduring-hearted\nOdysseus — that he shall return.
And I will go to Ithaca, to stir his son the more,\nand set strength of purpose in his heart
to call the long-haired Achaeans into assembly\nand speak out to all the suitors, who day upon day
slaughter his thronging flocks and\nhis shambling crook-horned cattle.
And I will send him to Sparta and to sandy Pylos
to ask after his dear father's\nhomecoming, if he may hear of it —
and so that good report among men may be his."
So she spoke, and bound beneath\nher feet the beautiful sandals,
ambrosial, golden, that carry her over the water and\nover the boundless earth with the breath of the wind;
and she took up her strong spear, edged with sharp bronze,
heavy, huge, and solid,\nwith which she breaks the ranks of men,
of heroes, when the daughter of\nthe mighty Father is angered.
Down she went, darting from the peaks of Olympus,\nand stood in the land of Ithaca at Odysseus' doorway,
on the courtyard's threshold,\nthe bronze spear in her palm,
in the likeness of a stranger:\nMentes, leader of the Taphians.
There she found the lordly suitors. They were pleasing
their hearts with counters, out in front of the doors,
sitting on hides of oxen they themselves had slaughtered,\nwith heralds and quick serving-men among them:
some were mixing wine and water in the great bowls,\nand some were wiping the tables down with porous sponges
and setting them out, and some carved meat in plenty.
Godlike Telemachus saw her far the first,\nfor he sat among the suitors, sore at heart,
seeing his noble father in his\nmind's eye: if only he would come
from somewhere, and make a scattering\nof the suitors through the house,
and take back his honor,\nand be lord of his own possessions.
So he brooded, sitting among\nthe suitors — and he saw Athena.
He went straight for the porch, indignant at heart
that a stranger be left standing\nat the door; and standing near her
he took her right hand,\nand relieved her of the bronze spear,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
"Welcome, stranger. Here you will\nfind kindness — and afterward,
when you have tasted supper,\nyou shall tell us what you need."
So saying he led the way, and Pallas Athena followed.
And when they were inside the high-roofed house,\nhe carried the spear to the tall pillar and set it upright
inside the polished spear-rack, where already other\nspears stood in numbers, enduring-hearted Odysseus' own;
and he led her to a high seat,\nspreading linen beneath her,
a beautiful seat, cunningly worked,\nwith a footstool for her feet.
For himself he set a painted bench\nbeside her, apart from the others,
the suitors, for fear the stranger, sickened by the din,
might lose all taste for supper, fallen among bullies —
and so that he might ask him about his absent father.
A handmaid brought water for their hands in a pitcher,
a beautiful golden one, and poured it over a silver basin
for them to wash, and drew up\na polished table beside them.
The grave housekeeper brought\nbread and set it before them,
laying out delicacies in plenty, giving gladly of her\nstore; a carver lifted platters of meat of every kind
and set them down, and placed gold cups beside them,
and a herald kept coming round to them, pouring the wine.
In came the lordly suitors, and they took their seats\nin order on the benches and the high-backed chairs.
Heralds poured water over their hands,\nslave-women heaped bread in baskets at their sides,
and young men crowned the mixing-bowls with drink,
and their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,\nthe suitors — other things now filled their hearts:
song and dance, for these are the ornaments of a feast.
A herald put the beautiful lyre into the hands of\nPhemius, who sang for the suitors under compulsion,
and he swept the strings and struck up his lovely singing.
But Telemachus spoke to gray-eyed Athena, leaning\nhis head close, so that the others might not hear:
"Dear stranger, will you take offense at what I say?
These men care only for such things — the lyre and song —
and easily, since unpunished\nthey devour another man's living:
a man whose white bones rot somewhere in the rain,\nlying on a mainland shore, or the salt wave rolls them.
But if they saw him once come home to Ithaca,\nevery man of them would pray to be quicker on his feet
rather than richer in gold and fine clothes.
But no — he has perished by an\nevil doom, and for us there is
no comfort left, not though some man upon the earth
should say he is coming still:\nhis day of homecoming is lost.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
What man are you, and from where?\nWhere are your city and your parents?
On what kind of ship did you come? And how did\nsailors bring you to Ithaca? Who did they claim to be?
For I hardly think you came here on foot.
And tell me this too, honestly, so that I may know it:
is this your first coming here, or are you from of old
my father's guest-friend? For many were the men who came
to our house — since he, too, went much among mankind."
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"Then I will tell you all of it, and truly.
I declare myself Mentes, son of wise Anchialus,\nand I am lord of the oar-loving Taphians.
Now I have put in here with my ship and my companions,\nsailing the wine-dark sea toward men of alien speech,
to Temese, after copper;\nthe cargo I carry is gleaming iron.
My ship stands off in the fields, away from the city,\nin the harbor of Rheithron, under wooded Neion.
Guest-friends of each other's houses we declare ourselves\nfrom the beginning — only go and ask the old man,
the hero Laertes, who they say comes no more to the city,\nbut far out in the fields endures his sorrows
with one old serving-woman, who sets his food and drink
before him whenever weariness takes hold of his limbs\nas he creeps along the rise of his terraced vineyard.
And now I have come. They said\nhe was here among his people —
your father. But no: the gods are thwarting his road.
For noble Odysseus has not yet died anywhere on earth;\nhe lives still, held back somewhere on the wide sea,
on a sea-ringed island, and hard men have him,\nsavages, who hold him there, I think, against his will.
And now I will prophesy to you, as the immortals\ncast it into my heart, and as I believe it will be —
though I am no prophet, no sure reader of birds.
He will not now be long away from his own dear\ncountry, no, not if iron chains should hold him:
he will find a way to come home,\nfor he is a man of many devices.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
whether you, grown so tall,\nare the son of Odysseus himself.
The likeness is uncanny — the head, the fine eyes.
We were often in each other's company, he and I,\nbefore he went up into Troy, where the others also,
the best of the Argives, went in the hollow ships.
Since that day I have not seen Odysseus, nor he me."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Then I will tell you, stranger, all of it, and truly.
My mother says I am his. For myself, I cannot know:
no man yet has been witness to his own begetting.
Would that I had been the son of some blessed man\nwhom old age overtook among his own possessions!
Instead, the man born unluckiest of mortal men —\nhis son, they say, I am. Since you ask me this."
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"The gods have not appointed your line to be nameless\nin time to come: Penelope has borne too fine a son.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
What feast is this, what gathering?\nWhat is your part in it?
A banquet? A wedding? For plainly\nno man here brought his own share:
so overweening, so past all bounds they seem to me,\nfeasting through the house. A man would burn with anger,
seeing shame upon shame — any man of sense who entered."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Stranger — since you ask me this and press the question —
there was a time this house promised to be rich and honored,\nwhile that man was still here among his people.
Now the gods have willed otherwise, plotting evil:
they have made him vanish as no other man has vanished,
no man on earth. For I would\nnot grieve so even for his death
had he gone down among his\ncompanions in the Trojans' country,
or in the arms of his friends,\nonce he had wound the war to its end.
Then the whole Achaean people would have built him a tomb,
and he would have won great fame in\ntime to come for his son as well.
Instead the whirlwinds have\nsnatched him away without glory;
he is gone — unseen, unheard-of — and to me he has\nleft anguish and lament. Nor is he all I have to mourn
and groan for: the gods have made me other bitter cares.
All the great men who hold power among the islands —\nDulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus —
and all who lord it through rocky Ithaca:
so many woo my mother, and wear this house away.
And she neither refuses the marriage she loathes,\nnor can she bring it to an end. And they eat on, wasting
my house. Soon they will tear me to pieces too."
Then, stung to anger, Pallas Athena spoke to him:
"Shame on it! Great indeed is your\nneed of the vanished Odysseus,
to lay his two hands on these shameless suitors.
If only he came now and stood at the outer doors of\nthe house, with helmet and shield and a pair of spears,
the man he was the first time I set eyes on him\nin our own house, drinking and glad at heart,
up from Ephyra, from Ilus son of Mermerus —\nfor Odysseus went there too, in his fast ship,
in search of a man-killing poison, so he might have\nit to smear on his bronze-shod arrows. Ilus would not
give it, for he feared the undying gods' displeasure;\nbut my father gave it him, for he loved him terribly —
the man he was then! Let that\nOdysseus close with the suitors:
quick would their fates be then,\nand bitter their weddings.
But surely these things lie on the knees of the gods:
whether he comes home and takes repayment, or does not,
here in his own halls. As for you, I charge you:\nconsider how you will thrust the suitors from the hall.
Come then, mark me now, and take my words to heart.
Tomorrow call the Achaean heroes into assembly and\nspeak your word to all, and let the gods stand witness.
Command the suitors to scatter, each to his own,\nand your mother — if her heart is stirred toward marriage,
let her go back to the hall of\nher father, that powerful man:
there they will make the marriage\nand set out the bride-gifts,
very many, all that should follow a beloved child.
To you yourself my advice is close\nand shrewd, if you will hear it.
Man a ship with twenty oars, the best there is,\nand go out asking after your long-gone father.
Some mortal man may tell you — or you may hear the Rumor
that comes from Zeus, which most\nof all carries word among men.
Go first to Pylos, and question noble Nestor;\nfrom there to Sparta, to fair-haired Menelaus,
for of the bronze-shirted Achaeans he came home last.
If you hear your father is alive and homeward bound,\nthen, ground down as you are, hold out one more year.
But if you hear that he is dead, that he is no more,\nthen come back to your own dear fatherland
and heap his burial mound,\nand over it pay the death-rites,
very many, as is fitting,\nand give your mother to a husband.
Then, when you have made an end of all this and done it,\ntake counsel in your mind and in your heart
how in your halls you are to kill the suitors,\nwhether by guile or in the open. It is no longer for you
to hold to childish things: you are past that age.
Or have you not heard what fame noble Orestes took\namong all mankind, when he killed his father's killer,
Aegisthus of the crooked counsels,\nwho cut down his famous father?
You too, my friend — and I see how tall and fine you are —
be brave, so that men not yet born will speak well of you.
But now I will go down to my fast ship and my companions,\nwho I think grow restless with waiting.
Let this be your own care. Take my words to heart."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Stranger, you say these things out of a kind heart,\nas a father to his son, and I will never forget them.
But come now, stay a while,\nthough you are eager for the road,
so that bathed first, your own heart gladdened,\nyou may go to your ship with a gift, rejoicing in spirit —
a costly thing, and beautiful, to be your treasure
from me: such things as dear\nguest-friends give their guests."
Then the goddess answered him, gray-eyed Athena:
"Hold me back no longer; I long for the road.
The gift — whatever your own heart bids you give me —\ngive it when I come again, for carrying home,
and choose one truly beautiful.\nIt will bring you its match in return."
So gray-eyed Athena spoke, and she was gone,\nflown up and away like a bird. And in his heart
she had set strength and courage,\nand brought his father to his mind
more even than before. And when he sensed it in his mind,
he was awed at heart, for he guessed she was a god.
And at once he went back among the\nsuitors, a man like a god himself.
For them the famous singer was\nsinging, and they in silence
sat and listened. He sang the Achaeans' homecoming,
the bitter one, that Pallas\nAthena laid on them out of Troy.
From her upper room she took into\nher heart the god-filled song:
Icarius' daughter, watchful-minded Penelope.
She came down the steep stairway of her house,\nnot alone: two handmaids came attending her.
And when she reached the suitors, shining among women,\nshe stood beside the pillar of the close-built roof,
holding her glistening veil before her cheeks,\na trusted handmaid standing on either side,
and in tears she spoke to the godlike singer:
"Phemius, you know many other spells for mortal ears,\ndeeds of men and gods, that singers make renowned.
Sit and sing them one of those, and let them drink\ntheir wine in silence. But break off this song,
this bitter song that forever wears away the heart
in my breast — for on me above all\nhas fallen grief past forgetting.
So dear a face I long for, remembering always,
the man whose fame goes wide through\nHellas and the heart of Argos."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Mother, why grudge the trusted singer his right to\nplease us however his mind is moved? Singers are not
to blame: Zeus, surely, is to blame, who gives to men\nwho eat bread whatever he wills, to each man singly.
There is no fault in him for\nsinging the Danaans' hard doom:
men will always give their louder praise to the\nsong that comes to its hearers newest on the air.
Let your heart and spirit steel themselves to hear it.
Odysseus was not the only one to lose his day of\nhomecoming at Troy: many other men were lost as well.
Go into the house and see to your own work,\nthe loom and the distaff, and command your handmaids
to go about their work. The word belongs to men —
to all men, and to me above all:\nmine is the power in this house."
In wonder, she went back into the house,\nfor she laid her son's clear-headed word to heart.
Climbing to her upper room with her serving-women,\nshe wept there for Odysseus, her dear husband, until
gray-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyelids.
But the suitors broke into\nuproar through the shadowy halls,
and every man of them prayed to lie beside her in bed.
And clear-headed Telemachus began to speak among them:
"Suitors of my mother, insolent past all bearing,
for now let us feast and take\nour pleasure — but with no more
shouting, since it is a fine thing to listen to a\nsinger such as this man is, with a voice like the gods'.
But at dawn let us go and take our seats in assembly,\nall of us, so I may declare my word to you outright:
get out of my halls. Go busy yourselves with other feasts,
eating your own goods, moving from house to house.
But if this seems to you the\nbetter thing, the more profitable,
that one man's living be destroyed and nothing paid,
then carve away. And I will cry\nto the gods who live forever,
in hope that Zeus may grant\ndeeds of requital come to pass:
then you would die inside this house,\nand nothing paid for you."
So he spoke, and all of them bit hard into their lips,\nmarveling at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
Then Antinous spoke to him, Eupeithes' son:
"Telemachus, surely the gods themselves are teaching\nyou to talk so high and speak with so much daring.
May the son of Cronos never make you king in sea-circled\nIthaca — though by blood it is your inheritance."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Antinous, will you take offense at what I say?
Even that I would be willing to take,\nif Zeus should give it.
Do you say kingship is the worst\nthing that can befall a man?
It is no bad thing to be king: at once a man's\nhouse grows rich, and the man himself more honored.
But there are other kings enough among the\nAchaeans in sea-circled Ithaca, young men and old:
let one of them have it, since noble Odysseus is dead.
But I will be lord of our own house and of\nthe slaves that noble Odysseus won for me."
Then Eurymachus, Polybus' son, answered him:
"Telemachus, truly these things\nlie on the knees of the gods:
which of the Achaeans will be king in sea-circled Ithaca.
Your goods you may keep, and be lord in your own house;
may the man never come who would strip your goods from you
by force, against your will, while Ithaca is yet lived in.
But I would ask you, best of men, about the stranger:
where does that man come from? What country does he claim
for his own? Where are his kin,\nthe plowlands of his fathers?
Does he bring some message of your father's coming,\nor did he arrive here pressing a need of his own?
How he leapt up and vanished in a moment! He did not wait
to be known — and yet his face was in no way base."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Eurymachus, my father's homecoming is lost.
I put no more trust in messages, wherever they\ncome from, nor give heed to any prophecy my mother
may seek, calling some diviner into the hall.
As for the stranger — a guest-friend\nof my father's house, from Taphos;
he declares himself Mentes, son of wise Anchialus,\nand he is lord of the oar-loving Taphians."
So spoke Telemachus. But in his\nheart he knew the deathless goddess.
And they turned to dancing and the loveliness of song
and took their pleasure,\nand waited for evening to come on;
and while they took their pleasure the black evening came.
Then they went home to bed, each man to his own house.
But Telemachus — where his bedroom was built high
off the beautiful courtyard,\nin a place with a clear view all around —
went up to bed, turning many things over in his mind.
Beside him, bearing blazing torches,\nwalked one whose thoughts were loyal:
Eurycleia, daughter of Ops, Peisenor's son.
Laertes had bought her long ago with his own goods,
when she was still in her first youth,\nat the price of twenty oxen,
and honored her in his halls as\nhe honored his faithful wife —
but never took her to his bed:\nhe shunned his wife's anger.
She it was who carried the blazing\ntorches beside him, and of all
the house-slaves she loved him most:\nshe had nursed him when he was small.
He opened the doors of the close-built room,\nsat down on the bed, and pulled his soft tunic off,
and dropped it into the shrewd old woman's hands.
She folded the tunic and smoothed it out,\nhung it on a peg beside the corded bedstead,
and went out of the room, drawing the door shut by its\nsilver handle, and slid the bolt home with its strap.
There all night long, wrapped in\nthe choice fleece of the sheep,
he pondered in his heart the road Athena had shown him.
